originalGroup.material:
Counting from the train

Last Saturday, Dad and I travelled to the coast by train. While he ____1____ (read) a newspaper, I watched the fields pass the window. I began counting sheep, but the train moved too fast for me to be sure of the number.

Dad suggested choosing something ____2____ was easier to count. We decided to record stations instead. I wrote each name as we arrived, then compared my list ____3____ the route map above the door. 

The map showed two stations with similar names. I nearly wrote the same one ____4____ (two). A passenger pointed out the different endings, and I corrected my note before the train left. 

At the coast, we bought sandwiches and sat on a bench. It was the ____5____ (windy) day of our short holiday, so we held the paper bags firmly. 

On the return journey, I wanted ____6____ (check) whether the order of stops was exactly reversed. It was, although a train on another service might have a different stopping pattern. I put ____7____ (I) list beside the map again.

The exercise had made an ordinary journey ____8____ (interesting) than I expected. I had not discovered anything unknown to the railway, but I had paid attention. There was ____9____ useful difference between looking through a window and deciding what to notice. The list became a small record of a day that otherwise might have passed very ____10____ (quick).

originalGroup.material:
The envelope of seeds

Our gardening club received an envelope of seeds from a neighbouring school. Nobody had written the plant's name on it. The teacher asked us not to guess ____1____ (careless), because an incorrect label could remain in our records long after the original question had been forgotten.

We sent a message to the school ____2____ had given us the envelope. While waiting for a reply, we placed the seeds in a dry cupboard. We did not put them into the ground or mix them with the three other ____3____ (packet).

Two days later, a teacher replied. The seeds came from a tall flower in their school garden, and she attached a photograph. She also admitted that she was not certain of the exact variety. Her answer was helpful, ____4____ it did not settle every detail.

We made a label saying where the seeds had come from and what remained unknown. Our teacher said this was ____5____ (honest) than inventing a precise name. 

When spring arrived, we planted a few in separate pots. Each pot ____6____ (number), so we could connect our notes with the right plant. 

After ____7____ (watch) the seedlings for several weeks, we sent new pictures to the neighbouring school. The students there were pleased to see ____8____ (they) gift growing in another garden. We still had questions, but now we had more ____9____ (inform) to discuss. The original blank envelope had led ____10____ a conversation between two clubs, rather than a confident mistake copied from one notebook into another.

Our class wanted to know how many students brought reusable lunchboxes to school. We had seen several on one table, but our teacher said that a few visible examples were not enough ____1____ (answer) a question about the whole school.

We prepared a short survey and asked permission to visit other classrooms. The first question was difficult ____2____ it combined two things: owning a lunchbox and bringing it that day. An owner might have bought canteen food.

After ____3____ (separate) the questions, we tried the survey with a small group. One student asked whether a reused food container counted.  We added a definition ____4____ everyone could read before answering.

The next week, we collected responses from the classes that had agreed to take part. Not every class was included. Our report therefore described all the ____5____ (student) who had responded, rather than claiming to speak for everybody in the school.

We checked the totals ____6____ (careful). One answer had been entered twice, and removing the duplicate changed the number. It corrected our record, not anyone’s behaviour.

The result was ____7____ (low) than I had expected from looking at that one table. My teacher reminded ____8____ (we) that expectation and measurement were different things. We wrote a short paragraph about the limits ____9____ our survey alongside the results. When the report ____10____ (display) outside our classroom, that paragraph appeared in the same size as the headline. We wanted the conditions of the result to be as easy to find as the result itself.
